meta.title: Latin A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Latin → English (see the Latin, recall the meaning) and English → Latin (see an English meaning, recall the Latin). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no examination publishes a graded Latin word list, and the Common European Framework of Reference describes living languages, so this deck borrows the framework's A2 band only as a SCOPE — the everyday topics whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — and is Folio's own list, not any examination's. 390 of the 750 words come from a vocabulary written for that scope, in the words of Roman life: the numbers to a thousand and the ordinals, the seasons and the parts of the day, the wider family, work and the trades, the market, money and weights, clothing, the rooms and things of a Roman house, meals and the kitchen, the buildings of a town, roads, carts and ships, the country and the farm, more animals, the body and health, school and writing, games and leisure, feelings and character, more describing words, words of place and manner, and the verbs of an ordinary day. The other 360 are the commonest remaining words of classical Latin, by their rank in the Dickinson College Commentaries Latin Core Vocabulary, and the cards are dealt by that rank, so the words a reader of Latin meets most often come first; the few the list does not hold follow, ordered by how often they appear in the Tatoeba corpus. Every headword is printed with its macrons, the marks over a long vowel (amō, rēgīna), and with its dictionary entry beneath it: a verb's principal parts (amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum), a noun's genitive and gender (rēx, rēgis m.), an adjective's three genders (bonus, bona, bonum). The 328 nouns and 226 verbs, and the adjectives and pronouns, carry their whole table behind the All forms fold — every case in both numbers; a verb's five indicative tenses, present subjunctive, imperative, infinitives and participles. Example sentences come with 740 of the 750 words, three apiece for 704 of them, with the word picked out in colour. The speaker reads Latin with an Italian voice, which gives the Italianate church pronunciation rather than the classical one, because almost no device has a Latin voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale, as a scope only. Frequency: the Dickinson College Commentaries Latin Core Vocabulary (Christopher Francese and others, 2012–13), CC BY-SA 3.0. Meanings, gender, principal parts, macrons and tables: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

But he said: My son shall not go down with you: his brother is dead, and he is left alone: if any mischief befall him in the land to which you go, you will bring down my grey hairs with sorrow to hell.
Igitur, si intravero ad servum tuum patrem meum, et puer defuerit ­ cum anima illius ex huius anima pendeat videritque eum non esse nobiscum, morietur; et deducent famuli tui canos eius cum dolore ad inferos.
Therefore, if I shall go to thy servant, our father, and the boy be wanting, (whereas his life dependeth upon the life of him,) and he shall see that he is not with us, he will die, and thy servants shall bring down his grey hairs with sorrow unto hell.
Ad quæ servus tuus pater meus respondit: Vos scitis quod duos genuerit mihi uxor mea. Egressus est unus a me, et dixi: Bestia devoravit eum! Et hucusque non comparet. Si tuleritis et istum a facie mea, et aliquid ei in via contigerit, deducetis canos meos cum mærore ad inferos.
Whereunto he answered: You know that my wife bore me two. One went out, and you said: A beast devoured him; and hitherto he appeareth not. If you take this also, and any thing befall him in the way, you will bring down my grey hairs with sorrow unto hell.

"This more, besides, I charge thee to obey, / if any faith to Helenus be due, / or skill in prophecy the seer display, / and mighty Phoebus hath inspired me true, / these warning words I urge, and oft will urge anew: / Seek Juno first; great Juno's power adore; / with suppliant gifts the potent queen constrain, / and winds shall waft thee to Italia's shore."

Et sint parati in diem tertium. In die enim tertio descendet Dominus coram omni plebe super montem Sinai.
And let them be ready against the third day; for on the third day the Lord will come down in the sight of all the people, upon Mount Sinai.
Quod cum vidisset socer eius, omnia scilicet, quæ agebat in populo, ait: Quid est hoc, quod facis in plebe? Cur solus sedes, et omnis populus præstolatur de mane usque ad vesperam?
And when his kinsman had seen all things that he did among the people, he said: What is it that thou dost among the people? Why sittest thou alone, and all the people wait from morning till night?

"O lux Dardaniæ, spes o fidissima Teucrum, / quæ tantæ tenuere moræ? Quibus Hector ab oris / exspectate venis? Ut te post multa tuorum / funera, post varios hominumque urbisque labores / defessi adspicimus! Quæ causa indigna serenos / fœdavit vultus, aut cur hæc vulnera cerno?"
"O light of Troy, our refuge! why and how / this long delay? Whence comest thou again, / long-looked-for Hector? How with aching brow, / worn out by toil and death, do we behold thee now! / But oh! what dire indignity hath marred / the calmness of thy features? Tell me, why / with ghastly wounds do I behold thee scarred?"
